Study design

We conducted an ecological panel study of 204 countries and territories in seven Global Burden of Disease (GBD) super-regions, covering 2005–2023. We described the burden of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and malaria, assessed spatial clustering and socioeconomic inequality, examined associations with external health financing, and modelled potential health losses under reductions in development assistance for health (DAH). The unit of analysis was the country-year; estimates therefore describe population-level associations rather than individual effects (Morgenstern, 1995). Reporting followed the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) and relevant STROBE recommendations (Stevens et al., 2016; von Elm et al., 2007). The GATHER checklist is provided in the appendix.
Data sources and linkage

We linked five public sources: GBD 2023, World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI), World Health Organization (WHO) indicators disseminated through the UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) database, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) Financing Global Health estimates, and Natural Earth boundaries (Apeagyei et al., 2025; GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators, 2025; United Nations Statistics Division, n.d.; World Bank, n.d.; World Health Organization, n.d.). Records were harmonised using ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes, GBD location identifiers and the GBD super-region hierarchy. Table S1 summarises source coverage; Figure 1 shows the analytical workflow.

Study populations

Descriptive analyses covered 204 GBD locations. Spatial analyses included 203 locations with Natural Earth polygons, excluding Tokelau. Financing analyses began with 168 locations outside the GBD high-income super-region; this geographical classification is not equivalent to World Bank low- and middle-income status. After covariate exclusions, the NTD panel included 153 locations. Malaria models additionally required a maximum age-standardised malaria DALY rate above 10 per 100 000 during 2005–2023: 78 locations met this threshold and 77 entered the complete-case panel. Inequality analyses required population data; the original Theil analysis also excluded zero-rate locations.
Burden outcomes

GBD 2023 supplied annual all-age DALY counts and age-standardised DALY rates for the combined NTD-and-malaria category and malaria during 2005–2023. NTD totals excluding malaria were obtained by subtraction. The 2023 cross-section additionally contained 19 individual NTD components, selected deaths and prevalence estimates, and published uncertainty intervals (UIs). The 19 component DALY counts reproduced the 2023 NTD total. Historical country-level extracts covered selected years, whereas super-regional trends extended from 1990 to 2023. Age-standardised rates were expressed per 100 000 population (GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators, 2025). Percentage changes and their UIs were imported from GBD rather than calculated from endpoint bounds.
Financing exposures

The primary exposure was external health expenditure as a share of current health expenditure (CHE), scaled per 10 percentage points. The secondary exposure was log(1 + external health expenditure per capita). WDI health-financing series derive from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED), which follows the System of Health Accounts 2011 (World Bank, n.d.; World Health Organization, n.d.). External expenditure includes bilateral, multilateral and philanthropic financing originating outside the country. Both exposures were lagged by 2 years to allow for programme implementation and reduce contemporaneous feedback; lagging alone does not resolve endogeneity (Bellemare et al., 2017; Bendavid & Bhattacharya, 2014). Monetary values were expressed in current US dollars.
Additional sources and data quality

WHO-reported indicators provided outcomes not obtained from GBD: the number of people requiring NTD interventions (SDG 3.3.5) and malaria incidence per 1000 people at risk (SDG 3.3.3) (United Nations Statistics Division, n.d.; World Health Organization, 2020). These were retrieved through the UN SDG database after the WHO API returned server errors. IHME Financing Global Health estimates for 1990–2030 were used to calibrate the funding-cut scenarios (Apeagyei et al., 2025). Estimated DAH fell from US$49.6 billion in 2024 to a preliminary US$38.4 billion in 2025, approximately 22%. Spatial analyses used Natural Earth administrative level 0 polygons at 1:50 million scale (Natural Earth, n.d.). After projection to Robinson coordinates (ESRI:54030), the scripts generated an interior representative point for each country polygon. Euclidean distances between these points defined the original spatial weights. GBD extracts were retained as raw CSV and JSON files; WDI and SDG series were retrieved through public APIs. Truncated requests were split into shorter year windows, and country-year coverage was checked after assembly. The GBD outcome panel contained 3876 observations (204 locations × 19 years), with no missing outcomes. Raw data, processed datasets and scripts are archived with the paper. Natural Earth records with missing ISO codes were matched using administrative codes. The supplied WDI extract covered 2005–2024; the panel retained 2005–2023. Table S11 lists indicator codes, definitions, transformations and lags.
Missing data

GBD outcomes and the GBD covariates including Socio-demographic Index (SDI), universal health coverage (UHC) effective-coverage index and lag-distributed income per capita (LDI) were complete. Missingness affected WDI series. In the modelling frame of 2688 country-years (168 locations, 2007–2022), missing values accounted for 15.1% of lagged external expenditure share, 8.2% of lagged domestic government health expenditure, 4.7% of sanitation coverage and 4.3% of drinking-water coverage (Table S10a).

Fourteen locations had no usable lagged external expenditure share in the modelling window: American Samoa, Bermuda, Cook Islands, Guam, Montenegro, Northern Mariana Islands, Niue, Puerto Rico, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Slovakia, Tokelau, Türkiye, Taiwan and the US Virgin Islands. Nicaragua also lacked sanitation and drinking-water observations. These exclusions reduced the eligible NTD sample from 168 to 153 locations.

We assessed associations between incomplete records and log NTD DALY rate, SDI, year and super-region using logistic regression with country-clustered standard errors. These diagnostics described observed missingness patterns but could not establish whether data were missing at random.

Within each country, interior WDI gaps were linearly interpolated without a maximum gap length; final observations were carried forward for at most 2 years. We did not extrapolate backwards or impute outcomes. Remaining incomplete records were excluded from each model. We reconstructed a model-specific flag from the observed input series, using exposure values 2 years before the outcome and contemporaneous sanitation and drinking-water values. This identified filled model inputs in 62 of 2287 NTD observations (2.7%) and 14 of 1187 malaria observations (1.2%).

Missing-data sensitivity analyses used observed model inputs only, restricted the sample to countries with complete observations throughout 2007–2022, and used multiple imputation (Honaker & King, 2010; Rubin, 1987; Sterne et al., 2009; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011; White et al., 2011). Excluding observations with the corrected model-specific filling flag produced the same sample as requiring observed inputs, so these checks are not independent robustness tests. The original imputation model used four WDI variables, LDI, UHC, SDI, year, the observed outcome and country means of observed covariates. Outcomes were predictors only.

The supplied multiple-imputation implementation used Bayesian ridge regression with posterior sampling, 15 iterations and 20 datasets. Missing country-level auxiliary means were replaced with the corresponding across-country median. It imposed no explicit bounds on percentage variables and recorded no convergence diagnostics. Estimates were pooled using Rubin’s rules (Rubin, 1987). Table S10b retains these original estimates as provisional pending imputation diagnostics; its variance summary is the proportion of total variance attributable to the between-imputation component, not a finite-sample fraction-of-missing-information estimate.

Cross-sectional exposures used the latest available observation during 2019–2023. Complete records were available for 169 of 204 locations globally; 145 remained after excluding the GBD high-income super-region. Table S9 describes the global complete-case comparison. The WHO NTD intervention-need proportion divided the 2023 count by the latest available WDI population value, so its denominator was not necessarily from 2023.

Scenario analyses used 2022 population where 2023 values were unavailable. Missing GDP per capita for South Sudan, Yemen and Eritrea was replaced by the study-sample median for monetary valuation only, not for DALY projections.
Model specification

NTD rates were natural-log transformed; malaria rates used log (1 + rate) to accommodate values approaching zero. NTD and malaria models were fitted separately. Covariates were selected a priori from aid–health studies and the WHO NTD road map (Bendavid & Bhattacharya, 2014; Mishra & Newhouse, 2009; World Health Organization, 2020). Models adjusted for log domestic government health expenditure per capita (lagged 2 years), log LDI, UHC effective coverage per 10 points, and basic sanitation and drinking-water coverage per 10 percentage points (GBD 2019 Universal Health Coverage Collaborators, 2020). SDI was excluded from the primary models because it incorporates income; it was used for inequality ranking and sensitivity analyses. Collinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors on within-transformed covariates; maximum values were 6.1 for NTDs and 6.4 for malaria. These were interpreted as diagnostics rather than against an absolute threshold (O’Brien, 2007).
Descriptive and inequality analyses

We summarised 2023 all-age DALY counts, shares of global burden and age-standardised rates by super-region, and changes in age-standardised rates from 2010 to 2023 (Table 1). Cause-specific estimates are provided in Table S2. Maps, heat maps and trend plots describe geographical and temporal patterns (Figure 2, Figure 3 & Figure 4). Socioeconomic inequality was measured using a population-weighted concentration index, ranking countries from lowest to highest 2023 SDI (Kakwani et al., 1997; O’Donnell et al., 2008; Wagstaff et al., 1991). The index equals twice the weighted covariance of the age-standardised rate and fractional socioeconomic rank, divided by the weighted mean rate. Negative values indicate concentration in lower-SDI countries. We obtained 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 2000 country-level bootstrap resamples using the percentile method.

We calculated the population-weighted Theil T index and decomposed it into between-super-region and within-super-region components (Table 2; Figure 5) (Shorrocks, 1980; Theil, 1967). The original calculation required positive rates and available population, yielding 199 locations for NTDs and 86 for malaria. A sensitivity analysis retained zero malaria rates among all 199 locations with population data, assigning zero to the limiting term 0 log (0).
Spatial autocorrelation

Spatial dependence was assessed before regression modelling (Anselin, 1988). We constructed row-standardised weights from the six nearest neighbours of each projected country representative point. This retained island states in the spatial analysis. Sensitivity analyses used four or eight neighbours and a 2500 km inverse-distance band (Table S7) (Anselin, 1988; Getis & Aldstadt, 2004). Global Moran’s I assessed clustering in log (1 + age-standardised DALY rate), with 9999 permutations for inference (Moran, 1950). We reported permutation p values and z scores. Analyses were repeated within the sample outside the GBD high-income super-region and, for malaria, within endemic locations. Local Moran statistics identified high–high and low–low clusters and high–low or low–high outliers (Anselin, 1995). Multiple testing across 203 locations was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure at q < .05 (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Cluster maps are shown in Figure 5.
Panel econometric models

The primary analysis used within-country variation to account for time-invariant country characteristics (Wooldridge, 2010). Cross-sectional ordinary least squares (OLS) with super-region fixed effects and a maximum-likelihood spatial error model provided between-country comparisons (Bendavid & Bhattacharya, 2014; Cavalcanti et al., 2025; Mishra & Newhouse, 2009). Cross-sectional models additionally adjusted for rural population share. NTD panel models included 153 countries and 2287 country-years during 2007–2022; malaria models included 77 countries and 1187 country-years. The preferred specification included country and year fixed effects, the 2-year-lagged financing exposure and the covariates listed above. We retained 2007–2022 as the original primary window and examined extension through 2023 in a post-review sensitivity analysis. Additional checks omitted UHC and excluded observations without matching UHC or LDI records in the supplied raw archive (Table S15). We compared pooled OLS, random effects, two-way fixed effects with country-clustered standard errors, correlated random effects (Mundlak), first differences, and fixed effects with country-specific linear trends (Bell & Jones, 2015; Mundlak, 1978; Wooldridge, 2010). Mundlak models included country means of time-varying regressors. Country-specific trends were removed from outcomes and regressors before estimation. Each estimator was fitted using both financing exposures.

Diagnostics comprised the Breusch–Pagan test for country-level heterogeneity, Hausman and cluster-robust Mundlak tests, Pesaran’s test for cross-sectional dependence, the Wooldridge test for serial correlation, and a modified Wald test for groupwise heteroskedasticity (Table S3) (Bell & Jones, 2015; Breusch & Pagan, 1980; Drukker, 2003; Greene, 2018; Hausman, 1978; Pesaran, 2021). The preferred two-way fixed-effects model used Driscoll–Kraay standard errors with a Bartlett kernel and bandwidth of 3 to address heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence (Driscoll & Kraay, 1998; Hoechle, 2007). Sensitivity analyses used bandwidths of 1, 2 and 4 and country-clustered standard errors. These checks assess inference sensitivity; they do not remove the limitations of a 16-year panel. For NTDs, coefficients and confidence limits were transformed as 100 × [exp(β) − 1] to express percentage differences in DALY rates. For malaria, this transformation applies to rate + 1 and approximates a percentage difference in the rate when rates are large relative to 1. For the per-capita exposure, multiplying the coefficient by log (2) estimates a doubling of expenditure plus US$1, not a doubling of expenditure itself. All coefficients were interpreted as conditional associations. Fixed effects do not remove time-varying confounding, and lagging does not establish causal identification (Bellemare et al., 2017; Imai & Kim, 2021). We assessed consistency across estimators rather than relying on statistical significance alone.
Additional spatial and predictive analyses
Spatial panel models

Models used row-standardised six-nearest-neighbour weights and maximum likelihood with the Lee–Yu fixed-effects transformation (Lee & Yu, 2010). Year effects were removed by cross-country demeaning. Analyses were restricted to balanced 16-year panels of 130 countries for NTDs and 71 for malaria. The intended SAR summaries are direct, indirect and total associations derived from the spatial multiplier (I − ρW)⁻¹ (LeSage & Pace, 2009) (Table S12).
Geographically weighted regression

GWR and MGWR examined the 2023 NTD association in 145 locations outside the GBD high-income super-region with complete inputs (Brunsdon et al., 1996; Fotheringham et al., 2017; Oshan et al., 2019). Financing exposure was mean external expenditure share during 2019–2022. The log NTD DALY rate and all four predictors (external share, UHC, log LDI and sanitation coverage) were standardised to mean 0 and SD 1. Models used an adaptive bisquare kernel. Bandwidths were selected by minimising the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc), using golden-section search for GWR and back-fitting for MGWR (Hurvich et al., 1998). MGWR estimated a separate bandwidth for each covariate. Local inference used the MGWR multiple-testing adjustment based on covariate-specific effective numbers of parameters (A. R. da Silva & Fotheringham, 2016). Fit was compared with global OLS using AICc and R² (Tables S6a–b; Figure 7C).
Predictive modelling

We compared elastic net, random forest and LightGBM for prediction of log NTD DALY rates during 2007–2023, using validation schemes that reflected the panel and spatial structure (Bergmeir & Benítez, 2012; Breiman, 2001; Ke et al., 2017; Ploton et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2017; Zou & Hastie, 2005). Elastic-net penalty strength and mixing proportion (0.1, 0.5 or 0.9) were selected by internal five-fold cross-validation. Random forest used 500 trees, a minimum leaf size of 5 and 50% of features at each split. LightGBM used 600 trees, learning rate 0.03, 15 leaves, and row and column subsampling of 0.8. Tree-model hyperparameters were fixed before test-set evaluation. In the supplied elastic-net implementation, scaling preceded internal cross-validation and ordinary internal folds did not preserve the grouped or temporal validation structure. These results require rerunning with preprocessing and tuning inside structure-appropriate training folds. All models used 13 features: both financing exposures, the five panel covariates, rural population share, out-of-pocket expenditure share, SDI, year, and two projected coordinate variables. Validation comprised random five-fold splits, grouped five-fold splits by country, leave-one-super-region-out validation, and temporal validation (training: 2007–2017; testing: 2018–2023). Random splits were included to illustrate potentially optimistic performance when countries appear in both training and test sets. Temporal validation included a linear benchmark with country fixed effects and a linear time trend, allowing extrapolation beyond the training years. Test-period covariates were observed, so temporal results describe conditional predictions rather than fully prospective forecasts. Numerical comparisons remain provisional pending consistent test samples and corrected nested tuning. Performance was assessed on the log scale using root-mean-square error (RMSE), mean absolute error and R² (Table S5; Figure 7B). Mean absolute Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values summarised feature contributions to LightGBM predictions in the full dataset (Lundberg & Lee, 2017). These were interpreted as model attribution, not causal effects.
Scenario modelling of development-assistance cuts

The original analysis used two conditional scenarios for annual health losses under external-financing reductions. Neither identifies a causal effect. Scenario estimates retained below, in Table 4 and in Figure 8 are provisional: the available data do not support the stated 19-cause NTD accounting calculation, and the malaria econometric conversion requires correction. The scenarios reduced each country’s external expenditure by 5–15% (mild), 19–26% (reference) or 40–60% (severe). The reference range encompassed IHME’s estimated 22% decline in global DAH between 2024 and 2025; the severe scenario represented larger reductions (Apeagyei et al., 2025; Cavalcanti et al., 2025). The same proportional cut was applied to 153 locations with financing data, using the latest available 2019–2023 financing baseline and 2023 burden and population.

The accounting script summed cause-specific changes in all-age DALYs per person between 2010 and 2023, truncated each country’s total gain at zero, and multiplied it by 2023 population, external expenditure share and the funding-cut proportion. This assumes that gains attributable to external financing equal its share of health spending and reverse proportionately after a cut. Five 2010 NTD cause baselines were absent from the supplied extracts: other NTDs, yellow fever, Ebola, Guinea worm disease and Zika. The script replaced these missing values with near-zero counts. That substitution is unsupported, and the resulting NTD projections cannot be treated as validated estimates. The econometric script recalculated external expenditure share as s(1 − c)/(1 − sc), where s is the baseline share expressed as a fraction and c is the proportional cut. It multiplied the share change in units of 10 percentage points by the preferred panel coefficient and applied exp (βΔx) − 1 to baseline all-age DALYs. For NTDs, this additionally assumes that an age-standardised association transfers to all-age counts. For malaria, the outcome is log(1 + rate), so this proportional count conversion is only an approximation and must be replaced by an explicitly defined rate-scale calculation.

Uncertainty was propagated through 4000 Monte Carlo draws (Briggs et al., 2012). The scenario code treated each published DALY point estimate as a log-normal median and set the log-scale standard deviation to [log(upper UI) − log(lower UI)]/3.92. Simulated draws were independent across countries and causes, with shared standard-normal draws between 2010 and 2023 in the primary analysis and independent year draws in sensitivity analysis. These are approximations from published summaries, not original GBD posterior draws, and generally do not reproduce both published bounds exactly. Each simulation sampled a funding cut uniformly within the scenario range and applied it to all countries. For the econometric model, coefficients were sampled from a normal distribution using the preferred estimate and Driscoll–Kraay standard error. Country estimates were summed within each draw to obtain super-regional and overall projections. We reported medians and 2.5th–97.5th percentiles; these intervals reflect the specified simulation assumptions. Projected DALYs were valued at one time each country’s GDP per capita in current US dollars, with 0.5 and 3 times GDP per capita examined in sensitivity analyses. These multiples provide an illustrative monetary valuation, not a cost-effectiveness threshold or an estimate of fiscal losses (Bertram et al., 2016; Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Marseille et al., 2015). The domestic financing gap was calculated at each scenario midpoint as external expenditure per capita × population × proportional cut, summed by super-region. This was expressed as a percentage of domestic government health expenditure to describe the increase needed to replace lost external funds (Table S14).
Sensitivity analyses

Sensitivity analyses examined alternative spatial weights and samples; financing exposure definitions; SDI substitution and WHO-reported outcomes; panel estimators and country trends; spatial models; missing-data strategies; and included versus excluded locations. Scenario analyses varied temporal dependence of burden draws, attribution of gains to external financing, and monetary valuation (Tables S7, S10b, S12 and S13).
Statistical software and reproducibility

Analyses used Python: pandas and NumPy for data management; statsmodels and linearmodels for regression and diagnostics; PySAL packages for spatial analyses; scikit-learn for imputation, elastic net, random forest and validation; LightGBM and SHAP for predictive modelling; and GeoPandas and matplotlib for maps and figures (Oshan et al., 2019; Rey & Anselin, 2007). The reproducible code cand be found on this GitHub repository. Random processes used fixed seeds (scenario seed: 20261007). Tests were two-sided at α = .05, with emphasis on estimates and 95% CIs. Code, processed datasets and execution instructions are provided in the appendix.
Ethics and role of the funding source

The study used publicly available aggregate data without individual identifiers. The institutional determination regarding ethics review, study funding and the funder’s role requires author confirmation.
